title: Climate of concern: The changing face of social movements in North Africa – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: North African social movements have shifted from demanding regime change toward local, environmental and socioeconomic grievances, and are increasingly turning against EU-backed renewable-energy projects that divert land and water from communities - a warning sign for the political durability of Europe's North African green-energy partnerships.

themes.theme: From political revolt to issue-based activism

insights.claim: North African activism has shifted away from demanding regime change - as seen in the 2011 Arab uprisings and Algeria's 2019 Hirak movement - toward practical, often locally based demands for better state services, mirroring a parallel shift in European engagement policy away from political reform and toward socioeconomic cooperation.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: EU policymakers and investors engaging North Africa should expect negotiating counterparts (both governments and civil society) to prioritize concrete service delivery over political reform conditionality.

insights.claim: Morocco's 2025 Gen Z protests began as a response to failures in maternity health care before broadening into wider calls for social justice, illustrating how narrow service failures can escalate into national movements.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: A specific, seemingly narrow public-service failure can be a leading indicator of broader social-unrest risk in North Africa.
insights.locator: The 2025 Gen Z protests in Morocco

insights.claim: A 2024 opinion poll found one in six North Africans had personally experienced harm from climate change (or knew someone who had) in the prior two years, and 71% see climate change as a threat.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: Quantifies climate-driven social pressure as a mainstream, majority public concern in North Africa, not a fringe issue.

insights.claim: North Africa is simultaneously among the world's most climate-vulnerable regions (drought, desertification, flash floods, water scarcity) and one of the most promising sites for renewable-energy generation given abundant sunshine and proximity to the European market, creating an inherent tension when green-transition projects fail to benefit affected local communities.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: Frames North African solar/wind capacity as both an EU energy-security opportunity and a political-risk liability if local benefit-sharing is neglected.

insights.claim: In Tunisia, local protests against toxic gas leaks from phosphate processing in Gabès (starting October 2025) snowballed into a mass movement that was still ongoing nearly a year later.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: A single industrial pollution incident can trigger sustained, year-long social mobilization in North Africa - a template for how localized environmental grievances scale.

insights.claim: Morocco's Ouarzazate solar megaproject has drawn anger from nearby communities specifically because of its high water consumption in a water-scarce region, showing that renewable-energy projects themselves can become flashpoints rather than universally welcomed development.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: Water-intensive solar technology choices carry distinct local political risk in arid host regions - a factor for project siting and technology selection due diligence.

insights.claim: In Tunisia, solar projects have prompted local opposition because they remove land from community use and reinforce regional inequalities, reflecting a broader pattern where communities fear renewable-energy land and water resources will be diverted to benefit wealthy elites and foreign investors.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: Land-use and equity concerns, not opposition to renewables per se, are the actual friction point - relevant to how foreign investors structure local benefit-sharing in project agreements.
insights.locator: As North African countries increasingly seek foreign investment

insights.claim: A maturing network of local environmental NGOs now operates across the region - Youth for Climate Tunisia (youth mobilization and digital campaigns), Egypt's Greenish (climate education) and VeryNile (fisher-led plastic recycling on the Nile), and Algerian community groups on water access and desertification.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: Identifies specific civil-society organizations that EU-funded initiatives or ESG-focused investors could partner with for on-the-ground legitimacy.
insights.locator: Such climate-related movements have sprung up

insights.claim: The EU's 2025 Pact for the Mediterranean pursues a 'partnership of equals' logic - supporting solar, wind and green hydrogen production that supplies clean energy to Europe while promoting North African development and lowering local energy costs - but the author argues this framing will fail to deliver stability unless local businesses and civil society are included in project design from the outset, not just national governments.
insights.speaker: Anthony Dworkin
insights.so_what: EU-backed renewable-energy investment in North Africa carries embedded political risk unless structured with local co-benefit design - a due-diligence flag for financiers and developers.
insights.quote: The EU must frame its projects in a way that gives local populations as much agency as possible, by breaking down barriers for small businesses and including civil society in project design and planning.
